la:noun:maeror.html:
maeror (moer-), ōris, m.
maereo
,
a mourning, sadness, grief, sorrow, lamentation, whether secret or open (class.): maeror est aegritudo flebilis,: maerorem minui; dolorem nec potui, nec, si possem, vellem,; : maerore se conficere,: maeror funeris,: orationis,: clausi in tenebris cum maerore et luctu,: esse in maerore,: jacere in maerore,: versari in maerore,: maerore macerari,: meus me maeror lacerat et conficit,: maerore consenui,: maeroris tabe confecti,: deponere maerorem atque luctum,: a maerore recreari,: perpetuo maerore senescere,.—In plur.: meorum maerorum atque amorum summam edictavi tibi,: Pol maerores mi antevortunt gaudiis,: mibi maerores (dabo), illi luctum, Enn. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 309 Vahl.): accedunt aegritudines, molestiae, maerores, qui exedunt animos,.

la:verb:maereo.gloss: to be sad or mournful; mourn, grieve, lament
senses: to be sad or mournful; mourn, grieve, lament
to mourn or lament over, bewail, bemoan
la:verb:maereo.html:
maerĕo (moer-), ēre (maerui, ; ;
part. gen. plur. maerentūm, ; dep. collat. form dub., Matius ap. Müll., where, for maerebar and mirabar of the MSS., Müller reads maerebat; and , where, for maerebamini, the best MSS. have maerebatis), v. n. and a. [root mis; Gr. μῖσος, μισέω; Lat. miser; cf. moestus].
Neutr., to be sad or mournful, to mourn, grieve, lament (class.; cf.: doleo, lugeo, angor): cum immolanda Iphigenia tristis Calchas esset, maestior Ulixes, maereret Menelaüs,: nemo maeret suo incommodo; dolent fortasse et anguntur,mourns over his own misfortune,: cum omnes boni abditi inclusique maererent,: vos taciti maerebatis,: homines alienis bonis maerentes,: qui (amici) tuo dolore maerent, Sulp. ap. : maereat haec genero, maereat illa viro,: sedatio maerendi,: intellectumque nihil profici maerendo, § 64.— Impers. pass.: maeretur, fletur, lamentatur diebus plusculis,.—
Act., to mourn over, bemoan, lament, bewail any thing (class.): filii mortem,; : mortem perditorum civium,: rei publicae calamitatem,: casum ejusmodi,: illud maereo,: talia maerens,thus lamenting,.—
With acc. and inf.: qui patriam nimium tarde concidere maererent,: corpora Graiorum maerebat mandier igni, Matius ap. Müll. N. cr.—Hence, maerens (moer-), entis, P. a., mourning, lamenting, mournful, sad: maerentes, flentes, lacrimantes, commiserantes, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 107 Vahl.): quis Sullam nisi maerentem, demissum, afflictumque vidit?: hunc cum afflictum, debilitatum, maerentem viderem,: nunc domo maerens ad rem publicam confugere possum,: interque maerentes amicos Egregius properaret exsul,: dictis maerentia pectora mulcet,: fletus maerens,mournful lamentation,.—Sup.: mater maerentissima, Inscr. Mur. 1229, 7.

la:noun:maestitia.html:
maestĭtĭa (moest-), ae, f.
maestus
,
a being sad or sorrowful, sadness, sorrow, grief, dejection, melancholy (class.): ex maestitiā, ex hilaritate, ex risu, etc.,: totis theatris maestitiam inferre,: esse in maestitiā,: maestitiae resistere,: sapientia est una, quae maestitiam pellat ex animis,: illa maestitia est, caruisse anno circensibus uno,.—Of inanim. things, gloom, gloominess, severity: orationis,: frigorum,.

senses: mournful, of or pertaining to mourning or sadness
la:adj:maestus.html:
maestus (moest-), a, um, adj.
maereo, q. v.
,
full of sadness, sad, sorrowful, afflicted, dejected, melancholy (class.).
Lit.: quid vos maestos tam tristesque esse conspicor?: id misera maestast, sibi eorum evenisse inopiam,; : cum immolanda Iphigenia tristis Calchas esset, maestior Ulixes, etc.,: maestus ac sordidatus senex,; : maestus ac sollicitus,: maestissimus Hector,.—Of inanim. and abstr. things: maesto et conturbato vultu,: maesta ac lugentia castra,: maestam attonitamque videre urbem,: maesta manus,: horrida pro maestis lanietur pluma capillis,: comae,: collum,: timor,.—Poet., with inf.: animam maestam teneri,. 775.—
Transf. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Like tristis, gloomy, severe by nature: ille neci maestum mittit Oniten, (naturaliter tristem, severum, quem Graeci σκυθρωπὸν dicunt ἀγέλαστον, Serv.): tacitā maestissimus irā,: oratores maesti et inculti,gloomy,.—
In gen., connected with mourning; containing, causing, or showing sadness; sad, unhappy, unlucky: vestis,a mourning garment, (4, 5), 13: tubae,: funera,; cf.: ossa parentis Condidimus terrā maestasque sacravimus aras,: a laevā maesta volavit avis,the bird of ill omen,: venter, exhausted with hunger, Lucil. ap. (enectus fame, Non.).—Hence, adv., in two forms. *
maestē, with sadness, saaly, sorrowfully: maeste, hilariter,.—*
maestĭter, in a way to indicate sorrow: maestiter vestitae,.

la:noun:Maeander.html:
Maeander (Maeandros or Mae-andrus), dri, m., = Μαιανδρος,
a river, proverbial for its winding course, which rises in Great Phrygia, flows between Lydia and Caria, and falls, near Miletus, into the Icarian Sea, now Mendere Su; nom. Maeander, ; ; ; ; ; : Maeandros,; ; : Maeandrus,; Paul. ex Müll.; acc. Maeandrum, ; : Maeandron,: more Maeandri,i. e. with turnings and windings,.—
Personified, acc. to the fable, the father of Cyane, and grandfather of Caunus and Byblis, .—
Transf. (from the windings of the Mæander), as an appellative, and hence also in the plur.
A crooked or roundabout way, a turning, twisting, winding, meandering, maze, etc.: quos tu Maeandros, quae deverticula flexionesque quaesisti?; ; cf. ; sqq.; ; : in illis dialecticae gyris atque Maeandris,: Maeandros faciebat et gyros, etc.,: Mĕandros,.—
In embroidery, a border wrought with many involutions or windings: victori chlamydem auratam, quam plurima circum Purpura Maeandro duplici Meliboea cucurrit,; cf. Serv. in loc.; cf. , and Paul. ex Müll.— Hence,
Maeandrĭus, a, um, adj., = Μαιάνδριος.
Of or belonging to Mæander, Mæandrian: juvenis Maeandrius,i. e. Caunus, the grandson of Mæander,.—
Of or belonging to the river Mæander, Mæandrian: unda,: flumina,.—
Maeandrĭcus, a, um, adj., Mæandrian (acc. to I. B. 2.): fluxus,—*
Maeandrātus, a, um, adj., full of curves like the Mæander, Mæandrian: facies Maeandrata et vermiculata, Varr. ap. (Sat. Men. 86, 14).

la:other:Maelius.html:
Maelĭus, a,
the name of a Roman gens, of which the most celebrated member is Sp. Maelius, who, under suspicion of aiming at kingly power, was slain, at the command of the dictator L. Quinctius Cincinnatus, by the magister equitum C. Servilius Ahala, ; ; ; ; cf. Aequimaelium.—Hence,
Maelĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mælius, Mælian: caedes, i. e. the murder of Sp. Maelius, .—Subst.: Maelĭāni, ōrum, m., the partisans of Mælius, Mælians, .
